editor_spans.body: Read together, this week's Ukraine statements show something the 'rock-solid support' language hides: energy prices are pushing British policy as much as solidarity is. The Prime Minister told the Commons that an energy ceasefire is 'the quickest way' to get diesel back onto world markets. The day after the US-Russia agreement, the government's response turned straight to energy markets and the cost of living. The Chancellor started his IMF pitch with a Middle East conflict that is 'hitting people across the world.'

This leaves London with a tension it has not resolved. It wants Russian energy income cut, through oil sanctions that now cover over 90% of capacity and a ban on shipping services for Russian LNG that it is urging partners to copy. It also wants energy supply back on the market quickly to ease prices at home. An energy ceasefire is the one policy that serves both aims, which is why so much has been staked on it. But within days of Trump calling for one, Russia was hitting energy infrastructure again. A plan that depends on that ceasefire depends on the cooperation of the very state it is trying to pressure.

The amounts are worth checking against the tone. 'Go further and faster' and 'double down' amount, for now, to speeding up £10 million of a £45 million missile delivery, inside a £1.6 billion commitment to LMM missiles over four years that already existed. The sanctions, military and fiscal packages are only things ministers have been 'asked to draw up.' Ukraine is heading into its fifth winter under bombardment. What matters is how much new money arrives in the next few weeks, not how firm the statements sound.

The biggest news in the 12 October statement was not about the UN. It was the Prime Minister saying Britain should hold 'a serious dialogue about the different options' for its long-term relationship with the EU, and calling the status quo a 'dereliction of duty.' A government has now formally reopened the question of where Britain stands in Europe. The promise that 'the British public will be the boss' hints at a public vote without saying so.

The way he made the case matters. It rests on the cost of border checks, not on arguments about sovereignty: Scottish salmon facing document checks on every shipment, up to £1,400 in costs on a single load, burgers and seed potatoes kept out of EU markets, and cheaper energy in Northern Ireland. Ten years after the referendum, the argument for closer ties is being made on supermarket prices and lost exports. That is ground where opponents find it harder to answer. The 20 November summit is the first test of whether the deal can deliver those savings.

Two announcements on the same day show what kind of Prime Minister Andy Burnham is. In Lanarkshire he offered Holyrood a 'new model of regional empowerment' and called the Scottish Government one of Europe's most centralised devolved administrations. In Derby he set up the head office of a rail body built to bring the railway under one national, publicly owned organisation. He is a former mayor who wants power pushed down to regions and cities. Yet his main nationalisation project gathers power in one place. Siting the head office in a regional city does not change where control sits.

The Scottish offer has a sharp political edge. The UK government is telling voters that Edinburgh holds on to too much power, and it is setting up channels to Scotland's regions through No10 North and the Scotland Office. Those channels go around the First Minister even while they are described as working with her.

The rail figures deserve a closer look. The head office will hold up to 450 staff and won't be finished until spring 2029. The 600 apprenticeships are spread over four years, about 150 a year. The real long-term problem is in the government's own figure: under 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25. An industry that old will lose skilled people faster than a foundation-level apprenticeship scheme this size can replace them.
